newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Islamic Jihad says it carried out Gaza bombings.
newsitem.headline: Islamic Jihad says it carried out Gaza bombings.

text.p: The military wing of the Palestinian Islamic Jihad group said on Thursday two Arabs killed in explosions in the Gaza Strip this week were suicide bombers on their way to attack Israeli targets.
The announcement signalled the return of one of the deadliest Islamist militant groups to suicide bombings against Israel after a more than a year lull in attacks.

In a leaflet faxed to an international news agency, the group known as Qasam or "Oath" mourned Abdallah al-Madhoun and Anwar al-Shabrawi, the two men killed in Tuesday's botched bombings, as "martyrs".
It said the attackers were avenging Israel's building of the a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem on a hilltop known as Har Homa in Hebrew and Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic.

The claim of responsibility came one day after Sheikh Abdallah al-Shami, an Islamic Jihad leader in Gaza, disavowed the bombings in the group's name and accused Israel of orchestrating the attacks to divert world attention from its settlement policy.
Jihad's military wing said Shami's comments, though made in good faith, were hasty.

"Our technical and engineering units assert that technical errors have occurred causing the explosive devices to explode before hitting the targets," the statement said. No Israelis were hurt but one blast wounded five Palestinians.
The Palestinian Authority, which had blamed Israel for one of the attacks, rounded up about 30 Jihad activists in Gaza.
Shami said Israel's secret service agencies orchestrated Tuesday's attacks in order to drive a wedge between the Palestinian Authority and its Islamic opposition.

Islamic Jihad, whose leader Ramadan Shallah is based in Damascus, Syria, is a strident opponent of Israeli-PLO peace moves. The group, though smaller than the Islamic Resistance Movement Hamas, has carried out some of the most lethal suicide bombings against Israel.
In January 1995, two Islamic Jihad suicide bombers blew themselves up at a bus stop in Beit Lid in northern Israel, killing 22 soldiers.
Nine months later, Jihad leader Fathi Shqaqi was gunned down by unknown assailants in Malta in what was widely believed to be an Israeli assassination.

Jihad and Hamas came under a heavy crackdown from the Palestinian Authority after four suicide bombings in the Jewish state in early 1996 killed 59 people and helped propel right-wing Likud leader Benjamin Netanyahu to power in Israel.
Shami told reporters at a Gaza news conference on Tuesday that Islamic Jihad had not abandoned "armed struggle" against Israel but said the time was not appropriate for such attacks.

"We in the military wing of Islamic Jihad regret the hasty judgments and statements issued in good faith by some symbols of the Islamic movement who are not linked and have no information about this action," the leaflet said.
